sections.h2: Buying the waste module is the largest single cost in both pathways

chart.title: Buying the waste module costs more than processing or collection
chart.sub: Cost per tonne of module waste, P1 (Mechanical), ₹.

sections.means: Waste procurement is 68% of P1's recurring cost and identical in P2, so the input price drives the loss.
sections.todo: Treat the waste-acquisition price as the policy target, through mandated hand-over from developers and insurers rather than open bidding.

sections.h2: Both pathways lose money on every tonne of solar waste they process

chart.title: Chemical recycling recovers more but still loses more per tonne
chart.sub: Net result per tonne of module waste, ₹.

sections.means: P2 recovers 23% more revenue than P1, but its processing cost is nearly double, so it still loses ₹12,341 a tonne.
sections.todo: Start the EPR collection-and-recycling targets from 2027, as CEEW recommends, rather than waiting for the 2034-35 storage window.

sections.h2: Both pathways break even only at waste-module prices well below market

chart.title: The market price for waste modules sits above both break-even points
chart.accent: Market rate for a waste module
rows: Market rate for a waste module

sections.means: P1 breaks even at ₹375 a module and P2 at ₹330, both well below the market rate of about ₹600.
sections.todo: Use the mechanisms CEEW models, such as extending EPR-certificate trading to copper, then silver and silicon, to close that gap.

sections.h2: India's installed solar fleet has grown more than fourfold since 2019

chart.title: Installed solar capacity rose from about 35 GW to 164.6 GW
chart.source: CEEW (Kale & Tyagi, November 2025); MNRE data via SolarQuarter; PV Waste Management in India (2021).

sections.means: Modules on 25–30-year hardware turn today's small waste stream into a much larger one, from a 2021 high scenario of 34 kt by 2030.
sections.todo: Set EPR collection and recycling targets now, before the fleet reaches end of life, as CEEW proposes.
